| [THEORY-058](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-058.md) v2 | Mental disorders are maintained by self-reinforcing causal loops rather than expressing a latent common cause, which is how they can outlast their triggers | Three traditions that do not cite one another for it put self-sustaining loops where a latent cause would be. Salkovskis, Sighvatsson and Sigurdsson ([LIT-538](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-538.md)) make it a threat meaning protected by the behaviour it drives. Kendler ([LIT-539](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-539.md)) finds causal loops across levels, from genes to culture. | [THEORY-097](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-097.md) | Long-range coordination in the human forebrain is carried by brief ripples that co-occur at distant sites: during them neurons co-fire more whatever the distance between them, and at retrieval they carry stimulus-specific reinstatement of encoding co-firing | Verzhbinsky, Daume, Cheng, Rutishauser & Halgren (2026), [LIT-633](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-633.md): in 1,373 single units from five bilateral forebrain regions of 35 epilepsy patients doing a Sternberg task, ripples (70–100 Hz, about 70 ms) co-occur between bundles at a median 5% at every tract distance from 71 to 223 mm, and unit pairs co-fire a median 34% more during co-ripples than in no-ripple periods, beyond a rate-only null and with no loss over distance. | [THEORY-178](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-178.md) v3 | In an ensemble of sign-consistent Boolean rules on the 87-gene core of E. coli's regulatory network, a transient knockout or overexpression of one gene can leave the network in a different attractor after release, and every gene that does so reaches a strongly connected component containing a positive circuit | Zhao, Wytock, Reynolds and Motter (2024), [LIT-854](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-854.md). | [THEORY-190](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-190.md) v3 | Under geometric coarse-graining of the S¹ hidden-metric network model, which merges blocks of r angular neighbours into supernodes linked if any of their members were, the supernodes' link probability approaches the S¹ form with β kept, κ′ = (Σκ^β)^{1/β}, μ′ = μ/r and R′ = R/r, its ratio to that form tending to 1 as their separation grows large against the block width and the coupling μκ′κ″; between nearby supernodes it exceeds that form | García-Pérez, Boguñá and Serrano (2017), [LIT-869](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-869.md): derived to first order, checked on one synthetic network over eight layers and on six real ones. The record proves the closure at large separation, with relative error of order β times the block width over the separation, and computes that between neighbouring supernodes the union of member links exceeds the S¹ form (by 32–86% in a worked example with two-node blocks). The source's flow ⟨k⟩′ = r^ν⟨k⟩, with ν = 2/(γ−1) − 1 or 2/β − 1, rests on the closure at every separation and is [QUESTION-203](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-203.md). | [THEORY-193](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-193.md) v2 | A simplicial complex grown by gluing each new d-simplex to one (d − 1)-face, by a rule that uses no geometry, has a 1-skeleton whose geodesic triangles are 2-thin at every size, so hyperbolic network geometry in Gromov's sense is an outcome of the combinatorial growth; the equal-link drawing as ideal simplices is a convention, a tiling of the hyperbolic plane for d = 2 in the manifold flavor but not a tiling of hyperbolic d-space for d ≥ 3 | Bianconi and Rahmede (2017), [LIT-867](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-867.md), read in [NOTE-678](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-678.md), for the model, the degree law and the ideal-simplex drawing. Every such complex has a 1-skeleton with 2-thin geodesic triangles, whatever the flavor, so its hyperbolicity is a property of the network. The constant-curvature picture, ideal simplices in the Poincaré ball, is a choice of drawing. It tiles H² for d = 2 in the manifold flavor, and for d ≥ 3 it is not a tiling. This says nothing about whether real networks grow this way. | Active |
| [THEORY-242](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-242.md) v2 | A spiral of silence can make a small, fixed minority opinion look far more widespread than it is without any member changing belief, and in the model that shows it the network's direct distortion of what members see is small | Vilone and Polizzi (2024), [LIT-939](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-939.md), read in full in [NOTE-810](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-810.md). | [THEORY-254](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-254.md) | Tangle-defined cohesion matches network communities only where community structure is strongly delineated, and tangles of one to three vertices recur beside the ones that do | Salter-Duke (2024), [LIT-955](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-955.md), a PhD thesis read in full in [NOTE-814](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-814.md). | [THEORY-276](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-276.md) v2 | In a network of identical units with identical couplings, the orbits of the graph's symmetry group are synchronization clusters, and a cluster moved only by its own factor of the group can lose synchrony while the others keep it | Pecora et al. The pattern of clusters that can synchronize is read from the wiring; whether each does is set by the dynamics through its own transverse block. Symmetry is sufficient, not necessary, for clusters. | [THEORY-321](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-321.md) v4 | Under repeated DeGroot averaging in a strongly connected society, the consensus converges to the truth as the society grows if and only if the largest influence weight vanishes, so network structure alone, not the members' common updating rule, decides whether the group belief is right | Golub & Jackson (2010), [LIT-999](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-999.md), Proposition 2 with Lemma 1, Corollary 1, Proposition 3 and Theorem 1, read in [NOTE-840](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-840.md) with the main proofs checked. | [THEORY-365](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-365.md) v3 | In one study of a stack of proximity graphs on nested random subsets of the data, each element's top layer drawn geometrically, greedy search on uniform random data in 8 dimensions needed a number of distance computations that grew no worse than logarithmically with the number of items and stayed below a single-layer navigable graph's at every size tested, and in 4 dimensions the beam width needed for a fixed recall saturated; the logarithmic bound is derived only for exact Delaunay graphs of bounded degree, which the index does not build, and on 200 million SIFT vectors the measured growth departs from it | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md) from arXiv v4. | [THEORY-370](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-370.md) | On an n × n lattice whose nodes also get long-range links drawn with probability proportional to lattice distance to the power −r, a searcher that knows only the target's position and the links of nodes already reached delivers in expected time polylogarithmic in n only at r = 2: greedy routing then takes O((log n)²) steps, while for 0 ≤ r < 2 every such searcher needs Ω(n^((2−r)/3)) steps and for r > 2 Ω(n^((r−2)/(r−1))), even at r = 0 where short paths exist | Kleinberg (2000), [LIT-1103](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1103.md), read in [NOTE-923](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-923.md). | [THEORY-385](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-385.md) v2 | In HNSW over 10-dimensional data in 100 isolated clusters, linking each new item to its nearest neighbours leaves part of the bottom layer unreachable from the entry point and caps recall well short of 1 however wide the query search, while linking a candidate only when it is nearer the new item than to any neighbour already kept keeps that layer connected and reaches recall near 1 with about half the links; on uniform data at 10 and 64 dimensions the two rules differ little; shown in Malkov and Yashunin's own tests on 10 million points and in an independent re-run on 30,000, which found the nearest-neighbour rule capped at a recall@10 of 0.72 to 0.83 against 0.999, at matched build cost too | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md). In HNSW, each new element's neighbours are chosen either as its M nearest candidates or by a pruning rule that keeps a candidate only if it is nearer the new element than to any neighbour already kept, a rule related to the relative neighbourhood graph. On 10M random d = 10 vectors in 100 isolated clusters, nearest-neighbour links failed to reach high recall and the pruning rule did not. In every test reported, the rule was at least as good. Its gain was largest at low dimension, at high recall, and on clustered data, and small on uniform or very high-dimensional data. These are the authors' benchmarks: one clustered dataset, synthetic, with no independent replication in this reading. Re-run independently at smaller scale on promotion (2026-10-20), with the same result. | Active |
| [THEORY-421](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-421.md) v2 | In HGCN embeddings of two synthetic 3-ary trees trained for link prediction or node classification, distance from the origin is only a partial reading of hierarchical level: the root is not innermost (distance 1.8–3.3 against a minimum of 1.2–2.4) and level order is recovered for 69–75% of node pairs; a loss built only on pairwise distances leaves the origin arbitrary | Yang, Zhou, Ying, Chen & King (2023), [LIT-871](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-871.md), read in [NOTE-669](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-669.md). | [THEORY-422](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-422.md) | In the standard formal models of group learning, no communication network is best for every epistemic problem: costly transmission favours minimally connected or star networks, pooling of estimates by averaging favours regular networks, and learning by trying in bandit problems can favour sparse ones, so a group's network cannot be judged until its learning problem is known | Zollman (2013), [LIT-716](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-716.md), a survey read in [NOTE-567](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-567.md). Under their idealisations the optimal structure changes with the problem, so neither "too little communication" nor unequal centrality is by itself an epistemic pathology. They predict that a transient crp knockdown leaves zraR, melR or rhaRS changed ([NOTE-655](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-655.md), C8, untested). [THEORY-178](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-178.md) is the model result this rests on. No such perturbation has been done in cells ([QUESTION-172](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-172.md)). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-799](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-799.md) | Under geometric coarse-graining of the S¹ hidden-metric network model the average degree flows as r^ν, with ν = 2/(γ − 1) − 1 when the degree exponent γ sets it and 2/β − 1 when β does, so the coarse-grained networks run toward a complete graph for γ < 3 or β < 2 and toward a ring otherwise | The degree flow that [THEORY-190](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-190.md)'s title carried before the promotion audit (batch 048) narrowed it to the asymptotic closure of the S¹ connection law. García-Pérez, Boguñá and Serrano (2017), [LIT-869](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-869.md), derive it to first order by treating the coarse-grained graph as an S¹ model at every separation. The record's exact computation shows that treatment fails between nearby supernodes, so the flow is unproved. Filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-803](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-803.md) | Real complex networks embedded in the hyperbolic plane are self-similar under geometric renormalization, their coarse-grained layers keeping the degree distribution, clustering and degree–degree correlations of the original, and this self-similarity is evidence that a hidden metric space underlies them | The empirical claim [THEORY-190](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-190.md) set aside when the promotion audit (batch 048) narrowed it to the model. García-Pérez, Boguñá and Serrano (2017), [LIT-869](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-869.md), find six embedded real networks self-similar under the renormalization and call this new evidence of hidden metric spaces. The collapse was judged by eye over two to five layers with no null ordering of the circle. Filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-815](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-815.md) | Layering a navigable small-world graph on nested random subsets of the data, with links separated by length scale and each layer's degree capped, makes greedy nearest-neighbour search cost grow logarithmically with the number of items on data of low intrinsic dimension, where the single-layer graph's cost grows polylogarithmically | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md), argue that HNSW's hierarchy is what makes greedy search logarithmic: constant cost per layer over O(log N) layers, against the polylogarithmic cost of their earlier flat graph. The record holds as measured, in [THEORY-365](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-365.md), logarithmic-or-better cost on uniform data in 8 dimensions and a saturating beam width in 4. The bound is derived only for exact Delaunay layers, which HNSW does not build, and on 200 million SIFT vectors the paper's own scaling departs from a logarithm, so the thesis is stated for low intrinsic dimension. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-825](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-825.md) | Hyperbolic graph embedding models trained on task losses that never mention the hierarchy do not place a tree's root nearest the origin, and their distance from the origin orders hierarchical levels only partly | Yang, Zhou, Ying, Chen & King (2023), [LIT-871](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-871.md), read in [NOTE-669](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-669.md), assert for hyperbolic graph models in general what they measured for HGCN on two synthetic trees: the root is not innermost and radius reads level only partly. The general form was the lead clause of [THEORY-421](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-421.md) until that account was narrowed to the measurement on 2026-10-20 ([ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4); it is filed here so that it stays a thesis evidence can confirm or reject. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-845](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-845.md) | In Weatherall, O'Connor and Bruner's network model a policy maker's credence depends on the evidence it has received only through the total excess of successes over failures of the new action, so a propagandist's effect is the excess of failures it adds; for the same pulls, running single-trial studies and publishing the failures adds at least as large an excess as any other division into studies, which is why biased production does best with the smallest studies | Weatherall, O'Connor and Bruner (2020; arXiv 2018), [LIT-1341](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1341.md), read in [NOTE-1038](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1038.md). With two symmetric hypotheses, each result's likelihood ratio depends only on successes minus failures, so the audience's belief is a monotone function of the cumulative excess; whoever chooses what the audience sees chooses that number. It holds for the paper's two-point hypothesis space and naive updating, and says nothing about richer hypothesis spaces or audiences that model the selection. | Active |
| [THEORY-855](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-855.md) | In Bala–Goyal network models of unbiased scientists testing a slightly better new action, a propagandist who forwards to Bayesian policy makers only those real results that favour the worse action can leave the policy makers near-certain of the false theory while the scientists converge on the true one; the effect weakens as the policy makers hear more scientists, as the better action's advantage grows and as each study gets larger | Weatherall, O'Connor and Bruner (2020; arXiv 2018), [LIT-1341](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1341.md), read in [NOTE-1038](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1038.md). No result is fabricated and no scientist is biased; the audience is misled because it updates on a selected sample as if it were not selected. It is a property of a stylized model, which the authors call "how-potentially"; it does not show that any real audience was misled this way, nor that an audience aware of the selection would be. | Active |
| [THEORY-887](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-887.md) | When an attribute is concentrated on well-connected nodes, many nodes can see it in a majority of their neighbours though it is globally rare, and the share that do grows with the correlation between degree and attribute, as the network becomes more disassortative and as its degree distribution becomes heavier-tailed | Lerman, Yan & Wu (2016), [LIT-1390](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1390.md), read in full in [NOTE-1085](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1085.md) from the PLOS ONE version. The "majority illusion": with 5% of nodes active, 60–80% of nodes in a heavy-tailed synthetic network can see an active majority among their neighbours; in disassortative real topologies, 60–70% with 20% active. A binomial model from the joint degree distribution predicts the share. The edge: the attributes are assigned by the authors on every network, real ones included, so this shows what topology permits, and nothing about what people perceive, believe or do. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-902](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-902.md) | In 30 four-person student groups discussing 15 choice dilemmas, a member's self-reported closure to influence on the next issue rose with their influence over prior outcomes, increasingly so along the sequence, and the groups' influence networks thinned and their discussions shortened while the rate of consensus did not change: evidence for a reflected-appraisal step by which influence concentrates in deliberating groups | Friedkin, Jia & Bullo (2016), [LIT-1482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1482.md), read in full from the CC BY version of record and its supplement in [NOTE-1126](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1126.md). Friedkin–Johnsen dynamics on each issue, not DeGroot. Closure and centrality both come from members' post-discussion chip allocations, and prior closure is not controlled. Supports the individual step and some structural trends; the predicted end state, one closed member and consensus on that member's view, was not reached. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-916](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-916.md) | In the DeGroot–Friedkin model, where a group reaches DeGroot consensus on each issue and each member's self-weight on the next issue equals their control over the last, with fixed relative interpersonal weights, self-weights converge from every non-autocratic start to one equilibrium ordered by the eigenvector centralities of those weights: power accumulates above a centrality threshold, is autocratic exactly when the network is a star and democratic exactly when it is doubly stochastic, and members whom no path of influence reaches end with none | Jia, MirTabatabaei, Friedkin & Bullo (2015), [LIT-1146](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1146.md), read in [NOTE-1135](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1135.md) from the version of record posted on the author's site; proofs skimmed. Theorems about a model, not findings about groups. The empirical companion, [LIT-1482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1482.md) ([THEORY-902](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-902.md)), uses anchored dynamics and a changing network, whose attractor is autocracy rather than this interior equilibrium. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-960](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-960.md) | In DeGroot's model, where each member repeatedly replaces its opinion by a fixed weighted average of all members' current opinions, F⁽ⁿ⁾ = PⁿF, the group reaches a consensus from every starting set of opinions exactly when the chain P has a single closed class of communicating members and that class is aperiodic; the consensus is then Σπᵢ Fᵢ with π the unique stationary vector, πP = π, which gives members outside the closed class no weight; two closed classes, or one periodic class, give no consensus | DeGroot (1974), [LIT-1527](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1527.md), read in [NOTE-1157](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1157.md). Repeated averaging with fixed weights is a Markov chain run on opinions, and whether it ends in agreement is a question about the chain's closed classes and their periods. It is not about how much each member trusts itself. The weights are fixed and no evidence enters, so nothing here says the consensus is right, and the periodic failure is a discrete-time one. | Active |
| [THEORY-993](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-993.md) | In the mixed membership stochastic blockmodel the probability of an edge from p to q, given the memberships, is (1 − ρ)π_pᵀBπ_q, so the graph's likelihood given the memberships is unchanged by π ↦ Rπ, B ↦ R⁻ᵀBR⁻¹ for any invertible R that keeps the memberships on the simplex and B in [0, 1], a continuum around any solution with B's rates strictly between 0 and 1; and the sparsity parameter ρ enters only through (1 − ρ)B, so it is fixed by nothing but the bound B ≤ 1, and the paper's printed estimator of it is the fraction of absent edges whatever the fit | Airoldi, Blei, Fienberg and Xing (2008), [LIT-1553](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1553.md), read in [NOTE-1179](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1179.md). The paper says the blockmodel and the memberships do not compete, because one is global and asymmetric and the other local and symmetric. Given the memberships they do: a change of block basis moves every node's memberships toward the centre and sharpens B, with the same edge probabilities. What can still separate them is the Dirichlet family assumed for memberships, not the graph. The confounding of ρ with B's scale is exact even in the marginal likelihood. | Active |
| [THEORY-1008](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1008.md) | Mixed memberships fitted by a fifteen-block MMSB to 871 yeast proteins' curated physical interactions carry information about the proteins' top-level MIPS functions beyond what the functions' base rates give: after mapping blocks to functions on 87 proteins, thresholded memberships predicted the other proteins' annotations with about 87% accuracy, against about 70% for random guessing at the right proportions | Airoldi, Blei, Fienberg and Xing (2008), [LIT-1553](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1553.md), §4.3.2 and Figs. 10–12, read in [NOTE-1179](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1179.md). The batch's one check of inferred mixed memberships against labels the model never saw. The reported margin is over a weak baseline, so it shows less than it seems: probably some information, not yet how much. It says nothing about whether the fifteen blocks are the fifteen functions. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1056](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1056.md) | In angular synchronization with outlier offsets, a polynomial-time spectral relaxation, the top eigenvector of the Hermitian matrix of measured phase offsets, recovers the angles once the share of good offsets exceeds about 1/√n on the complete graph, within a factor √((L − 1)/(2 log₂ L)) of the information bound that limits every algorithm, while exact maximum likelihood is a non-convex search costing O(mLⁿ) exhaustively; in this model the price of recovering the global configuration cheaply instead of optimally is a constant factor in evidence, which vanishes for L ≤ 6 | Singer (2011), [LIT-1655](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1655.md), §§2, 4 and 5, read in [NOTE-1224](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1224.md) from arXiv v2. The threshold p > 1/√n comes from a cited rank-one deformation theorem adopted to a non-Gaussian mixture and a heuristic comparison with random correlation, confirmed by simulation at n = 100 and 400; the near-optimality ratio compares it with an information bound for a different success criterion. Proposed for both steps. It does not say that recovery is cheap on every graph, under every noise model, or for fine angular resolution. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1059](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1059.md) | The dynamics a coupled cell network admits, restricted to a robustly synchronous pattern, are dynamics admitted by a smaller quotient network whose cells are the synchronized classes, so behaviour of the quotient, including symmetric behaviour the original network has no symmetry to force, appears in the original as synchronous behaviour; the quotient admits more dynamics than restriction produces, and is unique only up to refinement of its arrow types | Stewart, Golubitsky and Pivato (2003), [LIT-1674](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1674.md), read in [NOTE-1217](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1217.md): the quotient construction (§7), Theorems 8.3, 8.4 and 9.2 with proofs, the counterexample of Remark 7.5 and Example 7.1. Active as mathematics. The quotient describes the dynamics on the invariant subspace exactly, but only a subclass of the quotient's own admissible dynamics arises that way, and nothing is said about stability transverse to the subspace. | Active |
| [THEORY-1062](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1062.md) | On a discourse sheaf, where each agent expresses a private opinion through a linear map into each edge's space of topics, sheaf-Laplacian opinion diffusion converges to the orthogonal projection of the initial opinions onto the global sections, which are agreement in what each pair expresses and not in what they hold; stable polarized or incomparable private opinions are therefore possible, and when the sheaf has no nonzero global section the only limit is all opinions zero | Hansen and Ghrist (2020; SIAM J. Appl. Math. 2021), [LIT-1646](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1646.md), §§2–4, read in [NOTE-1222](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1222.md) from the arXiv preprint. Active as mathematics: the convergence is a theorem about a linear heat equation, and the gap between expressed and held opinion is in the definitions and is worked in an example. It does not say that people reach agreement this way, or that an agreement in expression shows anything about what is held. | Active |
| [THEORY-1065](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1065.md) | In a coupled cell network, a pattern of synchrony is invariant under every dynamics the network's architecture admits if and only if its partition of the cells is balanced, each cell of a class receiving, through each kind of arrow, the same number of inputs from each class; symmetry is one way to get balance and not the only one, so robust synchrony occurs in networks with no symmetry and among cells with no coupling between them, and the invariance says nothing about whether the pattern attracts | Stewart, Golubitsky and Pivato (2003), [LIT-1674](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1674.md), read in [NOTE-1217](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1217.md) from the accepted version: Theorem 6.5 with proof, Lemma 6.3, worked examples without symmetry (Figures 3, 9, 15, 19). Active as mathematics. It generalizes [THEORY-276](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-276.md)'s orbit clusters. "Robust" means invariant for the whole admissible class, not stable, and not invariant for one model family; the paper studies "existence, not stability". | Active |
| [THEORY-1070](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1070.md) | For a weighted cellular sheaf of finite-dimensional vector spaces on a finite cell complex, the kernel of the degree-k Hodge Laplacian is the k-th sheaf cohomology, in degree 0 the space of global sections, and the linear flow ẋ = −Δ^k x converges exponentially to the orthogonal projection of its initial state onto that kernel, each eigencomponent decaying at its own eigenvalue; the inner products on the stalks are part of the data, so the same sections can come with different rates, and the Laplacian does not determine the sheaf | Hansen and Ghrist (2019), [LIT-1659](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1659.md), read in [NOTE-1233](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1233.md) from arXiv v2: Theorem 3.1 (discrete Hodge theory), H^0 ≅ Γ (p. 7) and Proposition 8.1 (the flow), each with a proof; Fig. 3.1 for the Laplacian not determining the sheaf. Active as mathematics. The paper does not speak of relaxation rates or time-scale separation, does not say what produces the restriction maps, and treats only linear flows of a fixed Laplacian. | Active |
| [THEORY-1082](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1082.md) | On a connected graph whose edges carry phase shifts αᵢⱼ = −αⱼᵢ, the edge relations zⱼ = e^{iαᵢⱼ}zᵢ have a common nonzero solution, equivalently the twisted Laplacian Lα = δα*δα has a zero mode, exactly when the phase accumulated around every cycle is 0 mod 2π; otherwise each relation can be met alone but not all together, and the smallest eigenvalue of Lα, positive, measures the residual incompatibility, which on an isolated ℓ-cycle is largest at holonomy π | Torres-Hugas, Duch, Gómez and Arenas (2026), [LIT-1668](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1668.md), read in [NOTE-1218](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1218.md) from the arXiv preprint v2. The criterion is stated in the paper with an energy argument (pp. 2–3) and is the standard one for discrete magnetic and connection Laplacians, which it cites; the spanning-tree step the paper omits is written out below. The isolated-cycle spectrum is in closed form (eqs. 29–32). Both were checked numerically. Active: a theorem, with the qualification that it concerns the relaxed linear problem, not the phase dynamics. | Active |
| [THEORY-1087](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1087.md) | In the symmetric Sakaguchi–Kuramoto model on a triangle and a pentagon sharing one vertex, the lag α gives each ℓ-cycle a phase-independent path mismatch (ℓ − 2)α, and the remote-synchronized locked branch passes through an exact two-group state at α = π/3, where the pentagon's mismatch reaches π; but that branch has already lost transverse stability, in the pentagonal symmetry sector, at αc ≃ 1.0164, so the point of maximal cycle frustration marks the geometry of the phase relations, not the end of the synchronized pattern | Torres-Hugas, Duch, Gómez and Arenas (2026), [LIT-1668](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1668.md), read in [NOTE-1218](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1218.md) from the arXiv preprint v2. The mismatch (ℓ − 2)α is a three-line derivation (eqs. 15–18); the two-group state at π/3 is exact algebra (eqs. 38–40); the threshold αc is a numerical continuation with det M⊥ = 0 (Supplementary Material). All three were reproduced. Active for this motif and branch; the paper's wider reading, that remote synchronization is a manifestation of cycle-level constraints, is not what this says. | Active |
| [THEORY-1088](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1088.md) | When the expression maps of a discourse sheaf diffuse to reduce disagreement, with opinions held fixed they converge to the nearest sheaf, in Frobenius distance, of which the opinions are a global section, so apparent consensus is reached by changing what is said ("learning to lie"); with opinions diffusing too the joint flow is gradient descent on ½‖δx‖², and conserved diagonal blocks of αδᵀδ − βxxᵀ keep the opinions from collapsing to zero; nothing in either flow checks an expression against the opinion it expresses | Hansen and Ghrist (2020; SIAM J. Appl. Math. 2021), [LIT-1646](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1646.md), §§8–9, read in [NOTE-1222](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1222.md) from the arXiv preprint. Active as mathematics: Theorems 8.1, 9.3 and 9.4 and Lemma 9.1. Theorem 9.3's proof is right only for α = β as printed; with the α, β weights it holds generally, which was checked numerically in the reading. The degeneracy guards are internal to the loop: minimal change and a conserved quantity, not evidence from outside it. | Active |
| [THEORY-1090](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1090.md) | Eliminating an interior vertex of a cellular sheaf on a graph can leave its boundary a space of consistent assignments that no sheaf on the boundary vertices has: the interior can impose a constraint among boundary vertices that no set of pairwise compatibility conditions expresses, so Kron reduction, which turns the Laplacian of a connected graph into a graph Laplacian on any set of boundary vertices, fails for sheaves in general and holds when every vertex stalk has dimension at most one | Hansen and Ghrist (2019), [LIT-1659](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1659.md), §4.2 (pp. 18–21), read in [NOTE-1233](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1233.md): a worked three-leaf star with a two-dimensional centre, and a closure theorem for the scalar-stalk case. Active as mathematics; the argument was checked. It is about the space of sections, a static fact; it does not say how often the obstruction arises, what structure would express the reduced constraint, or anything about dynamics. | Active |
| [THEORY-1129](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1129.md) | Anchors entered as node features in fused Gromov–Wasserstein break a structural tie only when they move under it: with α strictly between 0 and 1, the zero-cost matchings of a structure with itself are exactly its automorphisms that fix every anchor, so a 6-cycle has 12 with no anchor, 2 with one anchor, 1 with two adjacent anchors and still 2 with two antipodal ones, and whether a set of anchors identifies the correspondence can be decided from the structure before any fit | Derived from Vayer et al. (2019), [LIT-1813](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1813.md), Theorem 3.2's zero case, read in [NOTE-1328](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1328.md); the paper does not state it. Checked by enumerating all 720 matchings of a 6-cycle with four anchor patterns. Active: an elementary consequence of a proved theorem, checked. It is about exact ties; with noisy data, symmetries become near-ties, and the theorem says nothing about how near. | Active |
| [THEORY-1130](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1130.md) | The Gromov–Wasserstein distance, half the least Lp distortion of a coupling, is a pseudometric on all networks with a probability measure on the nodes and any bounded edge weights, symmetric or not, and it is zero exactly when the two networks are weakly isomorphic, images of one network under maps that preserve weights and measures; so it compares only what the weight function and node measure record | Chowdhury and Mémoli (2019), [LIT-1822](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1822.md), read in [NOTE-1330](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1330.md) from arXiv 1808.04337v2. Theorems 16 and 18, with full proofs in the main text (pp. 8–9). Active: proved. The sharp edge is the zero set. A distance of zero says the recorded weights and measures agree up to merging and splitting nodes with identical profiles; it says nothing about relations the record leaves out, and the measure is chosen by the user. | Active |
| [THEORY-1132](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1132.md) | For K networks compared under square loss, the multi-marginal fused Gromov–Wasserstein objective of a joint coupling tensor is exactly the sum of the pairwise fused GW objectives of its two-way marginals, so the joint optimum is at least the sum of the pairwise optima, with equality exactly when some choice of pairwise optimal couplings is jointly realizable as the marginals of one tensor; a joint alignment is consistent in that sense by construction, which for deterministic couplings means the pairwise maps compose and for soft ones does not | Zeng et al. (2024), [LIT-1814](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1814.md), Theorem 1 and its proof (pp. 5, 12), read in [NOTE-1334](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1334.md). The identity was checked numerically; the equality condition and the remark on composition are the record's, short consequences of it. Active. The edge: "consistent by construction" means jointly realizable, not composable, once couplings are soft; and the paper never reports the gap that measures how far independent pairwise optima are from joint realizability. | Active |
| [THEORY-1139](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1139.md) | A graph network that learns its sheaf restriction maps from node features at each layer reaches the top of the standard small heterophilic node-classification benchmarks and stays within about one point of the best on homophilic ones; on a synthetic balanced bipartite graph it learns the negative transport the theory prescribes, but whether the maps it learns on real graphs have the geometry the theory credits for its success has not been examined | Bodnar et al. (NeurIPS 2022), [LIT-1811](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1811.md), §§5–6 and Appendix F, read in [NOTE-1332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1332.md). The results are empirical: Table 1 on nine datasets of 183 to 18,717 nodes with ten fixed splits, baselines copied from earlier papers, spreads of one to nine points; and one synthetic bipartite experiment in which the learned maps are inspected. Proposed: the paper's explanation of its accuracy, that the model learns the right geometry, is tested only on the synthetic case. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1140](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1140.md) | If every entity's O(d) frame may change independently and relation transports change as Tᵢⱼ ↦ gᵢTᵢⱼgⱼ⁻¹, then functions of the transports alone carry no invariant information except around cycles, a triangle's invariants are exactly the class functions of its holonomy H = TᵢⱼTⱼₖTₖᵢ, and an equivariant update of an edge from one cycle through it is Ψ(H)Tᵢⱼ with Ψ conjugation-equivariant; the symmetry fixes a family of updates, not one mechanism, and says nothing about whether a task has the symmetry | Sarkar, Mukherjee and Sato (2026), [LIT-1820](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1820.md), §2 and App. B, read in [NOTE-1331](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1331.md). The gauge-fixing argument is standard in lattice gauge theory and group synchronization, as the paper says, and its covariance was checked numerically here. Active: a conditional theorem. What it does not support is the paper's framing: "unique" holds for a family, and the antecedent is an inductive bias by the companion paper's own statement ([LIT-1803](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1803.md)). | Active |
| [THEORY-1141](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1141.md) | In the time limit, sheaf diffusion on a graph projects node features onto the harmonic space of its sheaf Laplacian, and which labellings that space can linearly separate depends on the class of restriction maps: a weighted graph Laplacian cannot separate the sides of a balanced bipartite graph, signed one-dimensional maps separate any two classes and no one-dimensional sheaf separates three, while diagonal maps with d ≥ C and orthogonal bundles with C ≤ 2d (d = 2, 4 and, against the paper, 8) separate any labelling; every separating sheaf is built from the labels | Bodnar, Di Giovanni, Chamberlain, Liò and Bronstein (NeurIPS 2022), [LIT-1811](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1811.md), §3.2 and Appendix B, read in [NOTE-1332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1332.md) from the arXiv preprint v4. Active as mathematics: each separation result has a proof, and Propositions 9, 10 and 13 were checked numerically. The paper says the orthogonal construction exists only at d = 2 and 4; it exists at d = 8 as well, by the Hurwitz–Radon theorem, and was built. The results are existential: the separating sheaf is defined from the class labels, so they say what a sheaf can do, not that one can be found without the labels. | Active |
| [THEORY-1147](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1147.md) | For entropy-regularized optimal transport with a fixed cost, the gradient of any differentiable function of the optimal plan with respect to the cost is obtained exactly from one linear system of size n + m whose matrix [[diag µ, T], [Tᵀ, diag ν]] is positive semidefinite and singular only along the gauge direction (1, −1), which does not affect the gradient; so the first-order effect of supervising any candidate pair on a utility of the whole alignment can be computed without forming the (nm)² Jacobian | Yu et al. (2026), [LIT-1807](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1807.md), Lemmas 4.2 and 4.3 with Appendix A (pp. 4–5, 14–17), read in [NOTE-1327](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1327.md). Proved by implicit differentiation of the optimality conditions; checked by finite differences. Active. It is a derivative: a local, first-order estimate of a finite change, exact only for plain entropic OT whose cost does not depend on the plan. | Active |
| [THEORY-1152](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1152.md) | Between two weighted directed networks with node measures, the Gromov–Wasserstein distance is bounded below by a hierarchy of invariants, each in an in-going and an out-going version, and the strongest of them, a transport problem whose costs are themselves transport problems, equals a transport problem whose costs are one-dimensional Wasserstein distances between the nodes' weight profiles, so it is computed in closed form; the bounds are one-sided, and two networks can agree on all of them while being at positive distance | Chowdhury and Mémoli (2019), [LIT-1822](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1822.md), Theorem 24 and Lemma 28 (pp. 11–13), read in [NOTE-1330](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1330.md). Proved; the equalities were already known for discrete spaces from Schmitzer and Schnörr 2013, as the paper says. TLB = R-TLB and the order of the bounds were checked numerically on 25 random asymmetric pairs. Active. The edge the paper leaves implicit: a zero lower bound is no evidence of sameness. A 3-node pair with every bound zero is at dN,2 ≥ 0.215 (the record's construction). | Active |
